summaries.example: Imagine that Maya could have learned to play the violin, even though she does not play it now. One view says this possibility is explained by Maya, who exists and could have been different. But consider a child Maya could have had but never did have. A possibilist says that such a merely possible child is part of reality in some way. An actualist says reality contains no such child; only actual people and things exist.
summaries.summary: The possibilism-actualism debate asks whether reality includes only things that actually exist or also things that could have existed. We easily understand some possibilities by thinking about actual things that could have been different. For example, an actual person might have climbed a difficult mountain route, even if they never did. But some possibilities seem to involve objects with no actual example, such as a child someone could have had but never had. Possibilists say that merely possible people and objects—called possibilia—are part of reality in some way. Actualists deny this and say that being and being actual are tied together. The source explains that the disagreement is about ontology, or what there is. It also describes different ways philosophers try to explain possibilities, including possible worlds, abstract states of affairs, properties, and special logical systems. The main challenge for possibilists is explaining why these unusual possible things should count as real. The main challenge for actualists is explaining how statements about possibilities can be true without such things.
key_ideas: People often agree that things could have turned out differently. The debate asks what makes those possibilities true.
Possibilists include merely possible people or objects in reality. Actualists reject these extra beings.
The debate is mainly about what exists, not simply about how we use words.
Possible-world ideas can help explain possibilities, but philosophers disagree about what possible worlds contain.
Some actualists try to explain possibilities using only actual things, such as abstract objects or descriptions.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us see that a question about an ordinary sentence—such as “someone could have had a child”—can lead to a deep question about reality. It also shows how ideas about existence affect logic, language, and explanations of what could happen. Learning the debate encourages careful thinking about what our claims assume.

important_terms.definition: A claim about what could be true or what could have happened.
The view that reality includes things that are not actual but could have been, such as a person who could have existed.
The view that there are no merely possible things; what exists is actual.
A thing that is not actual but could have existed.
A way things might have been different from how they are now.
A question about what kinds of things are part of reality.

questions_to_think_about: If something could have existed but never did, is it part of reality?
Is saying “Maya could have been a musician” different from saying “Maya could have had a child”? Why?
Can a story about a way things might have been explain what is really possible?
Which view seems more natural to you, and what would it need to explain?

summaries.example: Suppose a scientist, Lena, has never created a new species. It may still be possible that she could have done so under different circumstances. In that case, an actualist can appeal to Lena, an existing person, and say that she has a modal property: she could have created one. Now suppose Lena could have had a child, but in fact has no children. The possibilist says the possibility is grounded in a merely possible individual who could have been her child. The actualist must explain the truth of the claim without admitting that individual into reality. summaries.summary: The entry examines a dispute in metaphysics about whether reality contains merely possible individuals. Possibilism says that there are entities that are not actual but could have been actual. Actualism denies this, and the stronger actualist position says that there could not have been such entities. The debate begins with a contrast between two kinds of modal claim. An actual person could have had different properties, which can be explained by that same person’s modal properties. But a claim about someone who could have existed without actually existing seems not to be explainable in the same way. Possibilists broaden the domain of reality to include possibilia. They gain a unified account of modal truth, especially in possible-world semantics, but face the common-sense worry that merely possible people seem not to exist. The source also explains that bi-modal language is not essential: the dispute can be reframed using concreteness and contingent non-concreteness. In the formal system SQML, quantifiers range over a fixed domain across worlds. This validates the Barcan Formula and supports both possibilism and necessitism. Actualist systems instead allow world-relative domains or alter principles of quantification. Kripkean semantics, Plantinga’s haecceitist account, Prior’s strict actualist logic, and Adams-inspired perspectivalism represent different attempts to preserve an actualist ontology while explaining modal discourse. None is presented as an effortless solution; each changes how truth, reference, existence, or logical inference is understood.
key_ideas: The central issue is ontological: what exists in the broadest sense, not merely which formal language or inference is preferred.
Possibilism offers a direct truthmaker-style explanation of claims about merely possible individuals. Actualist approaches must explain those claims without accepting possibilia.
The traditional debate uses a distinction between actuality and mere possibility, but some philosophers recast it in terms of concreteness: actual things are concrete or necessarily non-concrete.

In simplest quantified modal logic, the Barcan Formula permits an inference from “possibly, something is F” to “something is possibly F.” This supports the possibilist strategy but also brings necessitism.

Kripke-style semantics allows the set of things existing at a world to vary. This blocks the Barcan Formula, but questions remain about whether the formal model has genuinely avoided possibilist commitments.

Actualist responses include haecceitism, strict actualism, and perspectivalism. They differ over whether modal truths must be grounded in individuals, properties, or propositions existing at every relevant world.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate shows how metaphysical commitments shape formal logic. A seemingly small question about whether someone could have existed can affect the interpretation of quantifiers, necessity, identity, and logical validity. It also illustrates a broader philosophical tension: a theory may offer elegant truth conditions while committing us to entities that seem unintuitive, or it may preserve common-sense ontology while accepting more complicated semantics or logic.

important_terms.definition: A thesis about what kinds of entities reality includes, especially whether it includes merely possible individuals.
The view that there are things that are not actual but could have been actual.
The denial of possibilism; in its stronger form, the view that there could not have been contingently non-actual things.
A merely possible entity: something that is not actual but could have existed.
The idea that reality has two modes of being, such as actuality and a less robust kind of being for the merely possible.
A possible entity understood as non-concrete but capable of having been concrete.
A formal interpretation using a set of worlds and a domain of individuals to evaluate modal claims.
The thesis that everything that exists is necessarily existent, in the sense that it could not have failed to exist.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining a possibility require a thing that has the relevant property in some possible world?
Why might the order of “possibly” and “something” matter in a sentence such as “Possibly, something is Lena’s child”?
Can a formal semantics be merely a useful reasoning tool, or must it describe what possible worlds and their inhabitants really are?
Is it acceptable to say that an individual could have failed to exist while also saying that some entity identical with that individual exists in every world?
Which actualist strategy best addresses both truth conditions and logical validity?

summaries.example: Think about a school play. Jordan could have been the lead actor, even though Casey was chosen. This possibility concerns an actual person, Jordan, who might have had a different role. Now imagine that Jordan could have had a younger sibling, although Jordan has no sibling. A possibilist may say that a merely possible sibling exists in some way. An actualist says there is no such sibling and must explain the possibility using only things that actually exist, perhaps by talking about different possible worlds or descriptions.
summaries.summary: The possibilism-actualism debate concerns the ontology of modality: what reality must contain in order for claims about possibility to be true. We can explain some possibilities using actual objects. An actual person, for instance, could have had different abilities or made different choices. But a claim that someone could have been the child of a person who has no children seems to require an individual who is not actual. Possibilists respond that reality includes possibilia, entities that are not actual but could have been. Actualists deny that there are such entities. The source emphasizes that actualism is more than the accidental claim that there happen to be no possibilia; it is the stronger claim that there could not have been any. Historically, this dispute was often described as involving two modes of being, actuality and mere possibility. Contemporary discussion can instead focus on concreteness: possibilia are contingently non-concrete, while actual things are concrete or necessarily non-concrete. Possible-world semantics makes the dispute especially sharp. In SQML, quantifiers range over one fixed collection at every world, so modal and ordinary quantifiers can exchange places in ways that support possibilism and necessitism. Actualist theories respond by varying world domains, interpreting worlds through actual abstract entities, or revising how truth and logical consequence are understood. The entry presents these as competing strategies for meeting the possibilist challenge, rather than as a settled solution.
key_ideas: The debate is fundamentally about what there is. It is not mainly a disagreement about vocabulary or about which symbols a logic should use.
Some possibilities concern actual individuals and are easy to explain through their possible properties. Other possibilities seem to concern individuals who never actually existed.
Possibilists accept possibilia to provide truth conditions for claims about such individuals. Actualists reject possibilia and face the task of giving an alternative explanation.
The bi-modal version of the debate distinguishes actuality from a weaker mode of being. Other philosophers avoid this distinction and describe possibilia as contingently non-concrete.
In SQML, the same domain of individuals is considered at every possible world. This makes certain exchanges between modal operators and quantifiers logically valid, including the Barcan Formula.

Actualist approaches change the semantics or logic in different ways. Kripke-style domains vary by world; haecceitism uses actual abstract essences as proxies; strict actualism may treat some modal claims as basic; perspectivalism distinguishes ways of evaluating truth at worlds.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic connects everyday counterfactual thinking with difficult questions about existence. It explains why theories of possibility cannot be separated completely from theories of logic: changing what counts as an available individual at a world changes which inferences are valid. The debate also teaches an important philosophical lesson about trade-offs between intuitive ontology, elegant semantics, and logical strength.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of what exists and what kinds of things belong to reality.
The view that reality includes merely possible individuals and objects as well as actual ones.
The view that reality contains no merely possible individuals; what exists is actual.
An individual or object that is not actual but could have existed.
A way the world might have been, used to discuss necessity and possibility.
A feature an actual thing could have had if circumstances had been different.
A formal method that evaluates statements by considering how they are true at different possible worlds.
The view that everything that exists could not have failed to exist.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “Jordan could have been the lead actor” easier to explain than “Jordan could have had a sibling”?
Does a possible world need to be a real place, or can it be an abstract representation?
Why would varying the individuals in a world block the inference from “possibly, something is F” to “something is possibly F”?
Should logic decide whether contingent beings exist, or should metaphysics decide which logic is appropriate?
What is gained and what is lost when an actualist rejects the demand for a compositional explanation of every modal claim?
